details:
**Magnitude and direction, contrasted with scalars**
The near-universal giveaway: a vector is a quantity with both a size (magnitude) and a direction, often drawn as an arrow. Scalars such as mass, temperature, or speed have only magnitude. Physical examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, and weight.

**Cross product and the right-hand rule**
An operation on two vectors that produces a third vector perpendicular to both. Its direction is found with the right-hand rule, it is anticommutative (a × b = −b × a), and it equals zero for two linearly dependent (parallel) vectors. A true cross product exists only in 3 and 7 dimensions, and in 3D it equals the Hodge dual of the wedge product.

**Dot product and orthogonality**
An operation on two vectors that yields a scalar, equal to the product of their magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them. Two vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) exactly when their dot product is zero.

**i-hat, j-hat, k-hat (unit vectors)**
The standard unit vectors, each of length (norm) 1, pointing along the x-, y-, and z-axes of rectangular coordinates. Any 3D vector can be written as a combination of these components. Projecting onto a unit vector gives the component of a vector in that direction.

**Parallelogram rule (tip-to-tail addition)**
Two vectors are added geometrically by placing them tip to tail, or by drawing them from a common point and completing a parallelogram. The diagonal of that parallelogram is the sum. Algebraically, this is the same as adding the vectors' components.

**Scalar triple product and the parallelepiped**
Combining the cross product and dot product of three vectors, a · (b × c), also called the box product, gives the volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are those three vectors.

**Gram-Schmidt process**
An algorithm that takes a set of linearly independent vectors and, by repeatedly subtracting projections, turns them into an orthonormal set (mutually perpendicular vectors of length 1). It is used to build orthonormal bases.

**Vector spaces, linear independence, and bases**
Vector spaces, the main subject of linear algebra, are sets of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication. A set is linearly independent if no member can be written as a linear combination of the others. A basis is a linearly independent spanning set, and the replacement (exchange) theorem shows every basis of a space has the same size, its dimension. Vectors are often written as row or column matrices.

**Hilbert and Banach spaces**
Complete vector spaces: a Banach space is a complete normed vector space, and a Hilbert space is a complete vector space with an inner product. Norms measure a vector's size; common ones are the L1, L2 (Euclidean), and L-infinity norms.

**Vector fields, gradient, divergence, and curl**
A vector field assigns a vector to every point in space. The gradient of a multivariable function is a vector of its partial derivatives that points in the direction of steepest ascent. Vector calculus uses divergence ("del dot") and curl; Gauss's law for magnetism sets the divergence of the magnetic field to zero. Conservative fields are gradients of a potential, and the line integral of a force field gives the work done along a path.

**Helmholtz decomposition theorem**
States that a sufficiently smooth, rapidly decaying vector field can be uniquely split into an irrotational (curl-free) part and a solenoidal (divergence-free) part. Equivalently, the field is determined by its divergence, its curl, and the boundary conditions.

**Hairy ball theorem (Poincaré-Hopf theorem)**
The hairy ball theorem says there is no continuous, nowhere-zero tangent vector field on a 2-sphere (you cannot comb a hairy ball flat without a cowlick). It follows from the Poincaré-Hopf theorem, which says the indices of a vector field's isolated zeros sum to the Euler characteristic of the surface.

**Gibbs and Heaviside, separating vectors from quaternions**
Vectors were originally treated as part of William Rowan Hamilton's quaternion algebra. In the late 1800s Josiah Willard Gibbs and Oliver Heaviside independently developed modern vector analysis as its own system.

**Eigenvectors**
A nonzero vector that a linear map only scales, so that Av = λv, where λ is the eigenvalue. Equivalently, multiplying the vector by (A − λI) gives the zero vector, the additive identity of the vector space.

**Cauchy-Schwarz inequality**
A basic inequality in inner product spaces: the absolute value of the inner product of two vectors is at most the product of their norms. In terms of the dot product, it amounts to the fact that the cosine of the angle between two vectors is between −1 and 1.
